summary: Three waves, each cut where the dependency graph closes. A is mail: the Google sign-in, the scheduler guardrails and the mail reader are built together with their first user, the morning digest. B opens the two kinds of outside content, web pages through a helper that holds nothing and then photos and PDFs, behind the roadmap's outbound gate. C adds what Happy keeps and does later: one house-rules check, reminders, notes, typed family facts and, if the family calendar is on Google, calendar questions and an evening text. Nineteen of the 42 cards are placed and 23 are left out; as the cards are written the three waves come to about 105 hours, which is five plans, and with the review's pending simplifications about 57 hours, which is three. Only wave B fits one plan both ways.

plan_size.basis: M1 ran 49 steps in nine phases whose own estimates add up to about 20 hours, so I counted steps phase by phase at about 25 minutes a step and added time where a sign-in, a soak period or a week of watching is involved; every figure here is my estimate, not a measurement.

The 07:00 text names the school item with its date in full and reaches only Tony, the hidden instructions cause no tool call and no second text, another person's agent asked for that mail gets nothing, and the firewall log shows the connector talking only to Google.

notes: Size, stated plainly: the 19 placed cards as written come to about 105 hours (41, 20 and 44), which is five plans, not three. With the pending simplifications named on each wave they come to about 57 hours (22, 15 and 20). Tony has confirmed none of those simplifications, so waves A and C are one plan each only if he says yes to S6, S9 and S14 for A and to S5, S8, S10 and S11 for C. Wave B fits either way.

Wave A is at the top of what one plan holds (about 48 steps). If it overruns, the two phases that can move to the start of wave B without touching the exit test are Jordan's inbox and the 'did I get an email about...?' lookup; the digest alone passes the exit test.

Wave A has two waits that work cannot shorten: the seven-day token check (T1) and a week of reading real digests. Publishing the sign-in app and signing in must happen on day one, and the wave cannot be switched on for real mail before Tony's answer on Q8.

Reading mail on the cloud model replaces the roadmap's rule that mail stays on a local model. That follows from Tony's own choices (local models skipped, mail wanted now), but the roadmap's mail exit test 'the reader makes no network calls' cannot hold as written; the firewall rule and the planted-mail test stand in for it, and the wave's exit gate records that in section 9.

The house-rules plugin is placed with its first user. Under the pending simplifications that is reminders, in wave C. If Tony wants the roadmap's second, coded check on who may call the mail connector (line 147) from the start, the plugin and T5 move into wave A (about 3 more hours) and Jordan's inbox or the lookup should then move to wave B.

Two tests have to be run twice because of the order. The lookup's seeded-mail test cannot show 'no hand-off to research' in wave A, where research does not exist, so wave B runs it again before web reading goes live. The hand-off canary in wave B protects very little until wave C renders real family facts, so wave C runs it again.
One convenience in a wave A card arrives later: the school digest's offer of a day-before reminder needs timed reminders, which are in wave C. The digest itself waits on nothing.

More than one new risk per wave could not be avoided in B and C without a fourth and fifth plan. In B, web reading and attachments go live in separate phases, each after its own test. In C, the scheduling tool, persistent notes and the calendar connection each go live in their own phase after their own test.

Waves B and C can swap. C needs B only for the flyer-photo route of F010, the hourly weather line in the evening text, and eval cases that plant instructions in a page or a PDF. If Tony would rather have reminders and notes before web reading, the order can change with those three points noted.

Almost everything in wave C hangs on answers Tony has not given (Q6, Q4, Q2, Q10). If he says no to reminders and the calendar is not on Google, wave C shrinks to typed facts and notes, about 10 hours. The cards that would then be next in line are the rest of the roadmap's research milestone, F049 (email to the asker) and F028 (trips), which need the house-rules check that wave C builds anyway.

I did not add a fourth wave. Tony's two 'advanced' examples, computer control and a connected iPhone, are the cards MAC-02 and OCL-01; both are marked experimental, each is a new high risk, and the roadmap puts anything that acts in the world last. Their gate (MAC-04) ships in wave B so that either can start a later plan.

The roadmap's S2 gate lists a Prompt Guard tripwire, which needs a local model runtime that is not in use. Wave B does not build it and asks Tony to put it off in writing; everything else in S2 is in wave B's first phase.
T9 belongs to the Reminders bridge and is not run in any wave. T10 is run only if Tony wants Jordan to restart Happy herself.
Hours and steps are my estimates from counting steps against the M1 runbook; the cards' own effort marks (S, M, L) have no unit and were not used as numbers.
